newsitem.title: USA: Enforcement aids municipal market - SEC official.
newsitem.headline: Enforcement aids municipal market - SEC official.

text.p: A top U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission official on Wednesday said the commission's recent enforcement actions in the municipal bond market should keep the market "healthy".

"The enforcement actions we bring assure that discipline will be maintained in this market with the hopeful result of a continuingly healthy market," Paul Maco, director of the SEC's office of municipal securities, said.
Addressing a conference on public finance in Marina Del Rey, Maco said the municipal bond market was already "healthy, and must be kept so through periodic weeding."
SEC enforcement activities in the municipal bond market have sparked considerable controversy, especially in California where several widely-reported probes of issuers are under way.

Dan Wall, a deputy director at the California State Association of Counties, said the SEC, before taking enforcement action, should take into account that public officials rely on the bond professionals they hire.
Municipal bonds are often "beyond the expertise" of elected officials in California, Wall said, adding, "Our form of government relies upon generalists."

Steve Juarez, a U.S. Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) board member, said he was concerned by the scope of recent SEC enforcement actions and probes, and called on the SEC to provide more guidance to public officials.
SEC standards need to "be placed in the context of local government," Juarez said, adding that more guidance by the SEC would help to lessen the anxiety felt by local officials.

Juarez said the association would draft guidelines to help public officials comply with municipal market rules. He said the association's report would be submitted to the SEC for review prior to its publication.
Maco said the SEC would work the the GFOA.
"We recognize that there is anxiety among some in the issuing community," Maco said. "We're very active, in my view, in trying to educate and relieve the anxiety."

"The overall goal here is not to slap people on the wrist with a ruler or make them clap the erasers," Maco said. "The overall goal is to enhance the communication that goes on between issuers and investors."
Maco said SEC enforcement actions are "often simply saying, 'that's bad disclosure, stop doing it.' At the same time, it also serves the broader role of instructing the rest of the marketplace."
Maco, Wall and Juarez spoke late on Wednesday as part of a panel at the Bond Buyer newspaper's California public finance conference.
